reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: A .415 xwOBA at the plate and a 2.70 xERA on the mound, from the same person, in the same season. The bat profile is nearly clean: 16.6% barrel rate, 15.3% walk rate, contact that grades out well on the expected side even with a 28.4% whiff rate that reflects how often pitchers make him chase rather than any real swing-and-miss hole. On the mound, the 98.1 mph fastball with 2486 rpm spin and a 30.4% whiff rate explains the xERA; the walk rate at 7.6% is the one place the pitching side still has room, and if that number drifts higher it compresses the ceiling there. The projection of 39 home runs and an .949 OPS across 691 plate appearances is what the Statcast profile reasonably supports, and the only real question is whether the Dodgers manage his pitching workload in a way that keeps both halves of this intact.

reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-six projected home runs from a 22-year-old, and the contact profile underneath it earns that number. Caminero's 93.4 mph average exit velocity sits at the 95th percentile, his hard-hit rate is 51.5%, and a 13.1% barrel rate shows the damage isn't just loud outs. What makes the projection credible at this age is the discipline: a 12.6% walk rate against an 18.3% strikeout rate is a genuinely rare combination, and it's the reason the .278/.358/.543 line holds together rather than collapses under swing-and-miss pressure. The OAA percentile is essentially the floor of the league, so everything rides on the bat staying this clean, because there's no defensive value cushioning a slump.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA is .314 and the xSLG is .526, which means the current .291/.481 projection isn't a ceiling, it's a floor with regression room built in. Witt's 53.2% hard-hit rate and 93.3 mph average exit velocity aren't soft contact flukes dressed up; they sit alongside a 16.5% strikeout rate that makes the contact profile genuinely sustainable at this volume. The one real tension in the profile is a 33.0% chase rate that lives well below average discipline, and if pitchers ever figure out how to bury him consistently outside the zone, the batting average is the first thing that softens. Add 47 projected steals to a .841 OPS at shortstop and you're looking at one of the five most valuable position players in baseball, full stop.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact-and-power combination here is genuinely unusual: a 22.9% barrel rate paired with a 17.0% walk rate produces a .432 xwOBA, and those two inputs almost never coexist at that level. The tension in the profile is the 29.0% strikeout rate, which sits well below the league median on the percentile card, but the chase rate is just 22.4%. He's not a free-swinger missing pitches he shouldn't see; he's missing pitches he does chase, and that's a more fixable problem. With a .618 xSLG and 95.3 mph average exit velocity both maxing the card, the underlying power is already operating at full volume, and if the strikeouts compress even a little, the projected .387 OBP and 39-homer ceiling aren't a stretch.

reports.name: Nick Kurtz
reports.published_report: The xwOBA sits at .383 and the walk rate is 18.7%, and together they explain why a 23-year-old first baseman with a 31.4% strikeout rate is still worth this much attention. He makes contact at a league-average clip by expected batting average, but when he does connect, 58.7% of balls are hard-hit and 18.4% barrel, two marks that put him at the very top of the sport. The entire profile hinges on whether that walk rate holds as pitchers learn him, because if they can tighten the zone and trim those free passes, the strikeouts turn from a tax into a debt. If it does hold, the projection's .908 OPS and 37 home runs are a conservative read on what the raw contact quality already suggests.

reports.name: Paul Skenes
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.74 and the xwOBA against is .259, both in the 93rd percentile, which puts the current production exactly where the eye test said it would land. What makes those numbers hold up is the combination: a 29.3% strikeout rate with a 5.5% walk rate means hitters are getting themselves out almost as often as Skenes is retiring them, and the barrel rate of 6.0% confirms that the contact being made isn't doing much damage. The projection calls for a 3.31 ERA over 184 innings with 221 strikeouts, a workload assumption that carries real weight given he's 23 and Pittsburgh will be managing him carefully. If the innings are there, this is a genuine top-of-the-rotation season.

What makes De La Cruz a legitimate everyday shortstop anyway is that 94.3 mph average exit velocity, a figure that sits at the 99th percentile, paired with a 14.5% barrel rate and 52.1% hard-hit rate that say the damage on contact is genuine and frequent. The .358 xwOBA and .476 xSLG give the projection's .266/.341/.469 line a real foundation, not a batting-average trick. If the strikeout rate ever compresses even slightly, this is a 25-homer, 29-steal shortstop who hits at the top of a lineup; if it doesn't, he's still that player, just one who makes the box score look uglier than the run total.

reports.name: CJ Abrams
reports.published_report: The chase rate is the friction point in an otherwise clean offensive profile. Abrams is running a 36.8% chase rate, a bottom-seventh skill that inflates his whiff numbers and caps his walk rate at 8.7%, yet the contact he does make carries real weight: 89.8 mph average exit velocity, a 9.9% barrel rate, and an xSLG of .438 that supports a projected 29 home runs from a shortstop who also projects for 27 steals. The Statcast contact grades, with xwOBA at .339 and xBA at .253, sit comfortably above average, meaning the underlying production is legitimate if he keeps squaring the ball up at this rate. If the chase rate climbs further and pitchers exploit it more aggressively, the walk rate shrinks, the strikeouts creep up, and what's left is a fast, occasionally explosive hitter who plays the position but doesn't quite force the lineup conversation; if the plate discipline holds where it is, he's a genuine middle-of-the-order piece at a premium spot.

His 97.8 mph fastball with 2487 rpm of spin gives it enough life that the strikeout rate isn't a surprise even when the 27.6% whiff rate looks modest against those other marks. The xERA sits at 2.92 on the current MLB sample, and the projection carries that conviction into a full season: 186 innings, a 2.65 ERA, 209 strikeouts, a 1.04 WHIP. reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: A 14.8% barrel rate with a 27.9% whiff rate is an unusual combination, and it's the whole argument for Sal Stewart. The barrels are genuine: his .473 xSLG sits well above his actual production, and an 11.3% walk rate means pitchers can't simply avoid the zone to neutralize him. What he isn't is a contact machine, the 50th-percentile xBA makes that plain, so the profile lives or dies on whether he keeps barreling the balls he does hit. If the barrel rate holds, the projection to 28 home runs and a .791 OPS at 22 looks conservative; if the whiff rate climbs and the barrels thin out, you're left with a below-average-contact first baseman whose speed won't save him.

reports.name: Pete Alonso
reports.published_report: The contact quality is elite and the exit velocity backs it up: 94.1 mph average and 54.4% hard-hit rate both sit in the 97th percentile, and an xwOBA of .375 says the underlying production is genuine. What keeps him from a true MVP conversation is the strikeout side, a 24.4% K% paired with a 27.5% whiff rate that both land below the median, and that tension between elite contact quality and below-average contact rate is the whole profile in miniature. If pitchers can reliably expand the zone against him, the projected .250 AVG stays a ceiling rather than a floor, and the power plays slightly beneath the .511 xSLG the batted-ball data suggests he should be running. Walk at 11.8% and slug .469 over 683 projected PA, and you have a near-certain 34-homer first baseman; the strikeout rate is the only thing standing between this profile and something meaningfully better.

reports.name: Aaron Judge
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile is a tale of two very different numbers: a 21.7% barrel rate sitting at the 100th percentile, and a 32.2% whiff rate that ranks 11th percentile. He hits the ball harder than almost anyone in baseball, and he misses more than you'd expect from a superstar, and those two facts have always coexisted in this profile. The .415 xwOBA and .600 xSLG are genuinely elite, but a 27.6% strikeout rate caps his floor — when the contact doesn't fall, there's no slap-hit safety net, just a .270 xBA and a lot of empty at-bats. At 33 with the projection calling for 416 PA, the real question is durability, because the underlying quality hasn't eroded; he's projected for 27 HR and a .931 OPS in what would amount to roughly two-thirds of a full season, and if he stays on the field the whole profile looks different.

reports.name: Ronald Acuña Jr.
reports.published_report: The .378 xwOBA tells you the bat is mostly there; the 14.8% walk rate, sitting at the 95th percentile, tells you the plate discipline never left. What's changed is everything else. Sprint speed at 27.3 ft/s and an OAA profile in the 10th percentile are the quiet reminders that this is a post-injury version of the player, and the projection's 28 stolen bases hinge entirely on whether his legs hold up across a full season. The power reads as genuine, a 13.1% barrel rate against an xSLG of .489, but a 29.3% whiff rate that ranks 25th percentile keeps the contact picture murky enough to cap the projection at .263/.379/.446 rather than anything that echoes his pre-injury peak. He can still be a dangerous offensive player; the ceiling here is a borderline All-Star, and the floor is a good-but-diminished regular whose value leans heavily on the walk rate holding the OBP line.

reports.name: Michael Harris II

He's an everyday center fielder with star-caliber contact talent and a plate discipline problem that keeps the full version of him just out of reach.

reports.name: Trea Turner
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is a study in contradictions held together by a single elite tool. His xwOBA sits at .282 and his xSLG at .355, both bottom-third of the league, and a 35.8% chase rate explains most of it: he's offering at too much and making weak enough contact that the underlying quality doesn't rescue him. The projection's .684 OPS reflects that honestly. What keeps him valuable at 701 projected plate appearances is the 30.0 ft/s sprint speed, a genuine 99th-percentile weapon that turns singles into doubles, routine outs into infield hits, and fuels the 29 projected steals. If the plate discipline doesn't tighten, specifically that chase rate, he's a speed-dependent second-division regular whose counting stats flatter a profile that's quietly eroding at the margins.

reports.name: Yoshinobu Yamamoto
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing a lot of the work here. At 5.3%, Yamamoto sits in the 92nd percentile in walk rate while his strikeout numbers are solid but not dominant, and that combination is what keeps the profile cleaner than the K% alone would suggest. His 33.8% chase rate explains why the walks are so rare even without overwhelming swing-and-miss stuff: hitters are expanding the zone, which limits damage more quietly than raw whiff volume does. The projected 2.86 ERA with a 1.0 WHIP is plausible because the contact suppression backs it up, a 3.31 xERA and 35.8% hard-hit rate that's better than it reads given the low barrel rate. The whole thing hinges on health and the ability to sustain that chase rate as hitters adjust to him in year two with the Dodgers; if the zone-expansion stops working, the modest strikeout rate has less margin to absorb.

At 3.6%, Skubal is practically in a class by himself for free passes allowed, and when you pair that with a 30.4% strikeout rate and a 36.3% chase rate, you get a pitcher who dominates counts, forces decisions, and almost never beats himself. reports.name: Seth Hernandez
reports.peak_summary: Projection: rotation starter with medium risk. The current pitching shape is bat missing over 38 IP.
reports.published_report: 14.6 strikeouts per nine innings across 66 A-ball frames is a number that makes you sit up, and the 2.60 ERA and 1.10 WHIP have held behind it. The miss grades out at the top of the minor-league pitcher pool, the walk rate grades out near the bottom, and that tension is the whole profile: a 30-grade command attached to an 80-grade arm. Translated to MLB context, the strikeout rate converts to a 9.5 K/9 while the walks land at 4.1, and the gap between those two numbers is exactly what the 30% K-BB% in the raw line is already telling you. If Seth Hernandez's command tightens even a tick, he's a rotation piece; if it stays here and the competition stiffens, he settles into a useful but limited big-league arm.

reports.name: George Kirby
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the engine here. He's not missing many bats, but he's not giving hitters clean counts to do damage in either, and the 6.7% barrel rate shows the contact he does allow tends to be manageable. When it holds, he's a mid-rotation workhorse who eats a full starter's workload and gives Seattle exactly what they need him to give.

reports.name: Jac Caglianone
reports.published_report: The contact metrics and the power metrics are pointing in completely opposite directions. His 93.7 mph average exit velocity sits in the 96th percentile and his 57.2% hard-hit rate climbs even further up the ladder, but a 30.1% strikeout rate at the 11th percentile and a 36.4% chase rate mean a lot of that violence never reaches a count where it matters. The .502 xSLG tells you what the contact looks like when he squares it; the projection's .256/.320/.454 line reflects what happens when you run that contact quality through a strikeout filter this aggressive. Everything here hinges on whether he can trim the chase enough to let the exit velocity carry a full season, because the floor without that adjustment is a pull-side masher who disappears against breaking stuff out of the zone.

reports.name: Andre Pallante
reports.published_report: The contact management is the whole argument here. Pallante runs a 6.2% barrel rate and 34.6% hard-hit rate, both sitting in the upper quarter of the league, while his strikeout rate of 17.6% and whiff rate of 20.8% are firmly below average. He's not missing bats, he's just keeping the ones he allows soft, and a 3.69 xERA says that's been a real and repeatable skill rather than a sequencing gift. The projection lines him up for a 3.87 ERA with 14 wins, which is a legitimate mid-rotation innings-eater if the contact suppression holds, but if hitters start squaring him up with any more authority, there's no strikeout floor to catch the fall.

reports.name: Emmet Sheehan
reports.published_report: The whiff numbers are loud enough to build around: a 30.8% whiff rate and a 35.0% chase rate are both well into the upper tier of the league, and those aren't the kind of numbers that evaporate when the sample grows. The problem is a 9.9% barrel rate that undercuts all of it — when contact does land, it lands hard, and that's why the xERA sits at 3.94 while a projected 4.52 ERA tells a different story about how games actually go. He misses bats at a rate most starters would take, but the barrel suppression isn't there to finish the job. If the contact management improves even modestly, he's a useful mid-rotation piece for the Dodgers; if it doesn't, he's a strikeout-heavy arm who keeps giving up enough damage to keep his rotation grip tenuous.

reports.name: Zack Wheeler
reports.published_report: A 2.70 xERA at 35 years old isn't a fluke waiting to happen — it's the shape of the profile explaining itself. Wheeler gets to that number through a 36.3% chase rate that keeps hitters perpetually off-balance, and he compounds the damage by limiting hard contact to an average exit velocity of 86.7 mph, meaning the barrels that do find him aren't finding much. The strikeout and walk numbers (29.4% K, 6.0% BB) form the spine of a true frontline starter, and the projection, 2.71 ERA, 190 strikeouts, 1.0 WHIP, follows naturally from what the Statcast profile actually says he is. The one dependency here is durability: if he stays on the mound, this is an ace season; if he doesn't, there isn't enough depth to the profile to rescue value from a partial year.

The 33.0% chase rate does the real work: he's not missing bats at a premium clip, a 24.8% whiff rate that grades out right near league average, so the whole profile hinges on whether he keeps generating those out-of-zone decisions as hitters get deeper looks. If the chase holds, he's a mid-rotation starter who outperforms his ERA; if the league adjusts and the swing decisions flip, a 24.5% strikeout rate without elite spin leaves very little margin.

reports.name: David Bednar
reports.published_report: The 40.6% chase rate is the headline, sitting at the very top of the league, and it explains most of what the Statcast card says about him. Hitters are expanding the zone against an elite rate, which suppresses hard contact even when they do make contact, and the 4.1% barrel rate is the result. The 28.6% strikeout rate and 30.7% whiff rate follow naturally from an arsenal that gets swings on pitches hitters shouldn't be chasing, and the xERA of 2.74 reflects a pitcher who profiles as a genuine high-leverage closer. The projection's 31 saves and 3.06 ERA over 65.9 innings is a reasonable translation of that profile, as long as the chase rate holds, because a walk rate sitting at 7.8% is the one lever that could complicate an otherwise clean picture.

reports.name: Chandler Simpson
reports.published_report: Zero barrels in his current MLB sample. He's a 38-steal, 1-homer outfielder whose value lives entirely in the legs and the bat control, and if either slips, what's left is a soft-contact singles hitter with a 5.4% walk rate and nowhere to hide.

reports.name: Freddy Peralta
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a puzzle: a 3.75 xERA with contact quality that looks genuinely suppressed, built almost entirely on spin rather than velocity. His barrel rate sits at 5.0% and average exit velocity at 87.8 mph, both comfortably better than league average, and 2422 rpm on the fastball explains how a 94.1 mph heater still generates weak contact. The strikeout rate at 22.0% and chase rate at 29.2% are both below average, meaning he's not missing bats at volume — he's winning by limiting damage when contact happens. That's a fragile blueprint: if the spin-driven soft contact dries up, a 4.37 ERA projection with a 1.36 WHIP and only 10 quality starts becomes the floor, not a conservative estimate. reports.name: Griffin Jax
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a puzzle with one loud piece and one ugly one. His 31.5% whiff rate and 33.7% chase rate say he can miss bats at a meaningful level, and 2526 rpm on his fastball spin sits at the 95th percentile, which explains how the swing-and-miss generates. The problem is what happens when contact lands: a 10.9% barrel rate and an xERA of 5.10 say hitters are doing serious damage when they connect, and that gap between a projected 3.67 ERA and the underlying contact quality is the whole tension in the profile. If Jax can keep hitters off the barrel while living off the chase and whiff numbers he's already producing, the 3.67 ERA version holds; if not, you're looking at a high-leverage reliever whose stuff plays better in shorter stints where the barrel luck can't accumulate.

reports.name: Brock Wilken

reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one live wire in an otherwise difficult profile. Wilken is drawing walks at a 17% clip in AAA, which translates to a 12.9% MLB-equivalent rate, well above the 8.5% MLB average, and that approach grade is the only above-average tool in a skill set being dragged down by a .179 average and a 30% strikeout rate over 304 plate appearances. reports.name: Jacob deGrom
reports.published_report: The tension in this profile is right there in the contact numbers: a 34.4% whiff rate sitting next to a 44.0% hard-hit rate and an average exit velocity of 90.7 mph. That's a pitcher who misses bats at an elite level but gets hurt when hitters do connect, and the xERA of 3.44 is roughly where the two forces settle. The strikeout rate at 30.4% and a walk rate of just 5.5% mean he's still commanding the zone the way only a handful of starters can, and at 97.2 mph on the fastball there's no diminishment story yet. The honest dependency here is health, a 37-year-old coming off multiple elbow procedures, and the projection calls for meaningful innings — if he stays on the mound, a mid-rotation-to-above-average season is on the table; if he doesn't, nothing else in the profile matters.

A 43.0% hard-hit rate and 90.3 mph average exit velocity are both bottom-fifth marks, which means the good underlying results are running almost entirely through a 96.3 mph fastball and a 27.3% whiff rate doing enough damage before contact happens. The strikeout rate sits at 24.5% with a walk rate of 7.2%, a combination that's functional but not dominant enough to carry him if the contact numbers stay this loud. If the whiff rate holds and the fastball keeps missing bats early in counts, he profiles as a solid mid-rotation piece, but the whole thing hinges on whether he can keep limiting damage on balls in play, because the contact quality suggests luck is doing some of the work right now.

reports.name: Will Sanders
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is bat missing over 40.3 IP.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing the carrying here. Sanders posts a 3.6 BB/9 across 48 innings split between A+ and AAA, and translated to MLB context that holds at 3.5, nearly indistinguishable from the 3.2 MLB average — close enough that command isn't the thing to worry about. The strikeout rate is the honesty: his 9.9 K/9 at the level translates to exactly league-average whiff rate, which means the profile lives and dies on whether the command edge keeps runners off base while the stuff isn't overwhelming anyone. If it does, he's a functional depth starter who eats innings and doesn't walk the ballpark; if the command slips even modestly, there's no swing-and-miss floor to catch him, and the 1.4 WHIP with a 45-grade run prevention shape tells you where the ceiling stops.

reports.name: Blake Mitchell
reports.peak_summary: Projection: low-end everyday regular with low risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 320 PA.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing real work here. Mitchell is drawing a free pass in 24% of his plate appearances at A+, which translates to a 15.3% MLB-equivalent BB% while the league average sits at 8.5%, and the .406 OBP is the direct result. The 35% strikeout rate is ugly and the .214 average isn't hiding it, but the ISO sits at .223 with 14 home runs in 320 PA, and when the translation lands those two tools together the profile reads as more than the batting average suggests. Everything hinges on whether the contact rate improves enough to keep pitchers from simply attacking him at the upper levels, because if it doesn't the walk rate alone won't sustain a lineup spot. A low-end everyday regular is the ceiling, a reserve role is the floor, and ValuCast has him moving up +4.3 in three days as the full picture comes into focus.

reports.name: Jarren Duran
reports.published_report: The .297 xwOBA is the inconvenient truth at the center of this profile: Duran runs a 29.7% strikeout rate and chases 35.0% of pitches outside the zone, and contact quality that would rate out near league-average in a vacuum gets annihilated by how rarely he makes contact at all. The speed is genuine, 29.2 ft/s at the 93rd percentile, and a 11.3% barrel rate suggests real pop when he connects. But the whiff rate sits at the 5th percentile, which means the projection's .218 AVG and .283 OBP aren't pessimism — they're what falls out when those contact numbers meet a full schedule of 631 PA. If the chase rate comes down even modestly, the barrel rate and speed give him a path to something more useful; if it doesn't, he's a 20-homer, 24-steal second-division regular whose value lives almost entirely in the counting stats.

reports.name: Hunter Brown
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one number that breaks this profile in half. Brown's 27.3 K% is genuine — strikeouts come from a 25.0 Whiff% that sits right at the median, paired with a 5.4 Barrel% and an average exit velocity of 85.2 mph that ranks in the 96th percentile, meaning hitters who do make contact aren't doing much damage. But a 13.3 BB% that ranks in just the 9th percentile poisons all of it, and the 25.6 Chase% explains why: he isn't getting batters to expand, so the zone is doing the work, and when he misses he misses badly. The xERA of 3.41 suggests the underlying contact suppression is real enough to survive some of that command volatility, which is why a 3.55 ERA projection over 101 innings is plausible, but if the walk rate climbs further rather than regresses, that projection dissolves into a back-end innings absorber rather than a mid-rotation asset.

reports.name: Francisco Lindor
reports.published_report: The .742 OPS projection is the quiet alarm in this profile. For a shortstop who built his reputation on being a complete, above-average offensive player, that's a number that belongs to a second-division regular, not the face of a franchise. The Statcast card shows sprint speed at 26.7 ft/s, a 33rd-percentile reading that explains why the 11 stolen bases in the projection feel like a ceiling rather than a floor. What keeps this from being a straightforward decline story is the 79th-percentile fielding grade, which means he's still earning his roster spot through defense even as the bat fades. Over 448 projected plate appearances, the question isn't whether Lindor can stay healthy — it's whether the .418 SLG holds enough to make him more than a glove-first shortstop who hits sixth.

reports.name: Alex Bregman
reports.published_report: The disconnect between his discipline and his damage is the whole profile. Bregman chases just 21.1% of pitches outside the zone, one of the better marks in the league, and his 16.6% whiff rate is similarly clean, yet his 4.5% barrel rate and 87.7 mph average exit velocity say the bat-to-ball skill isn't translating into leverage. The Statcast profile looks like a guy who wins the at-bat and then doesn't do enough with it, which is why a .315 xwOBA sits in the 42nd percentile and the projected .719 OPS feels more honest than harsh. If the power thins to 16 home runs over a full season at 32, what's left is a high-contact, high-walk third baseman with above-average defense, which is still a useful regular, just not the middle-of-the-order piece the Red Sox years suggested he'd remain.

reports.name: Taylor Ward
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole profile. Ward's 16.5% BB% sits at the 98th percentile, and his 14.7% chase rate leads every percentile card Statcast publishes — that discipline is what inflates a .344 xwOBA well above what his 5.9% barrel rate and middling exit velocity would otherwise produce. The contact quality is genuinely ordinary, but he manufactures value by simply refusing to swing at bad pitches, which is a real and repeatable skill. The projection's .364 OBP against a .377 SLG tells the story cleanly: he's a patient, low-power outfielder who earns his way on base rather than doing damage when he gets there. If pitchers eventually solve the passive approach and start attacking him in the zone, the contact quality doesn't give him much of a fallback.

reports.name: Ian Happ

He finds pitches to take and then struggles to make contact when he swings — a profile that caps his average at a projected .223 even when the barrel rate (13.1%, 82nd percentile) is legitimately generating power. The .320 xwOBA sits roughly at league average, which is the honest summary: a patient hitter who barrels the ball often enough to project for 27 home runs but leaves so much contact damage on the table that the overall offensive line (.330 OBP, .426 SLG) is solidly average rather than good. If the whiff rate ever comes down, you have a legitimately above-average outfielder; if it doesn't, he's a second-division regular whose walk rate and pop keep him in lineups without ever rising above them.

reports.name: Konnor Griffin
reports.published_report: Thirty-six projected steals on a .729 OPS is the whole tension here. Griffin's sprint speed sits at the 99th percentile, a legitimately elite tool, and the projection leans into it hard. The contact and power profile underneath it are another story: a 38.8% chase rate, a 31.7% whiff rate, and exit velocity in the bottom third of the league paint a picture of a teenager who hasn't learned to slow the game down yet. If the plate discipline tightens, there's a real offensive player in there, a second-division regular who makes pitchers pay with his legs; if it doesn't, the speed becomes a stolen-base specialist's résumé stapled to a lineup liability.
